claim: Malaria causes hundreds of thousands of annual deaths due to Plasmodium falciparum parasites.
source: Malaria remains a serious global health problem, with hundreds of thousands of annual deaths due to Plasmodium falciparum parasites.
evidence: This is a statement about the global health burden of malaria, presented as established fact in the introduction.

claim: There is an absence of a potent, long-lasting vaccine for malaria.
source: The absence of a potent, long-lasting vaccine and parasite tolerance to frontline artemisinin combination therapies continue to challenge malaria elimination efforts.
evidence: This statement reflects current scientific knowledge about the state of malaria vaccine development.

claim: Parasites have developed tolerance to frontline artemisinin combination therapies.
source: The absence of a potent, long-lasting vaccine and parasite tolerance to frontline artemisinin combination therapies continue to challenge malaria elimination efforts.
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about antimalarial drug resistance.

claim: The COVID-19 pandemic may disrupt malaria prevention and treatment efforts in Africa and cause a surge in malaria deaths.
source: Furthermore, there are strong concerns that the current COVID-19 pandemic will disrupt malaria prevention and treatment efforts in Africa and cause a surge in malaria deaths that unravels decades of progress (Weiss et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Weiss et al., 2020.

claim: Tetracycline antibiotics like DOX kill P. falciparum parasites by inhibiting prokaryotic-like 70S ribosomal translation inside the apicoplast organelle.
source: Tetracycline antibiotics like DOX are thought to kill eukaryotic P. falciparum parasites by inhibiting prokaryotic-like 70S ribosomal translation inside the essential apicoplast organelle (Figure 1; Dahl et al., 2006).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by citation to Dahl et al., 2006.

claim: Stable P. falciparum resistance to DOX has not been reported.
source: Although stable P. falciparum resistance to DOX has not been reported, clinical use is largely limited to prophylaxis due to delayed activity against intraerythrocytic infection (Conrad and Rosenthal, 2019; Gaillard et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Conrad and Rosenthal, 2019 and Gaillard et al., 2015.

claim: Clinical use of DOX is largely limited to prophylaxis due to delayed activity against intraerythrocytic infection.
source: Although stable P. falciparum resistance to DOX has not been reported, clinical use is largely limited to prophylaxis due to delayed activity against intraerythrocytic infection (Conrad and Rosenthal, 2019; Gaillard et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Conrad and Rosenthal, 2019 and Gaillard et al., 2015.

claim: Parasites treated with 1–3 µM DOX continue to grow for 72–96 hr and only die after the second 48 hr intraerythrocytic growth cycle.
source: Parasites treated with 1–3 µM DOX, the drug concentration sustained in human serum with current 100–200 mg dosage (Newton et al., 2005), continue to grow for 72–96 hr and only die after the second 48 hr intraerythrocytic growth cycle when they fail to expand into a third cycle (Dahl et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Newton et al., 2005 and Dahl et al., 2006.

claim: Current 100–200 mg DOX dosage sustains 1–3 µM drug concentration in human serum.
source: Parasites treated with 1–3 µM DOX, the drug concentration sustained in human serum with current 100–200 mg dosage (Newton et al., 2005), continue to grow for 72–96 hr and only die after the second 48 hr intraerythrocytic growth cycle when they fail to expand into a third cycle (Dahl et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Newton et al., 2005.

claim: Slow antiparasitic activity is believed to be a fundamental limitation of DOX and other antibiotics that block apicoplast-maintenance pathways.
source: Slow antiparasitic activity is believed to be a fundamental limitation of DOX and other antibiotics that block apicoplast-maintenance pathways (Gaillard et al., 2015; Dahl and Rosenthal, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gaillard et al., 2015 and Dahl and Rosenthal, 2007.

claim: First-cycle anti-Plasmodium activity has been reported for DOX and azithromycin concentrations > 3 µM.
source: First-cycle anti-Plasmodium activity has been reported for DOX and azithromycin concentrations > 3 µM, but such activities have been ascribed to targets outside the apicoplast (Dahl et al., 2006; Yeh and DeRisi, 2011; Wilson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dahl et al., 2006; Yeh and DeRisi, 2011; Wilson et al., 2015.

claim: First-cycle activities of DOX and azithromycin at concentrations > 3 µM have been ascribed to targets outside the apicoplast.
source: First-cycle anti-Plasmodium activity has been reported for DOX and azithromycin concentrations > 3 µM, but such activities have been ascribed to targets outside the apicoplast (Dahl et al., 2006; Yeh and DeRisi, 2011; Wilson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dahl et al., 2006; Yeh and DeRisi, 2011; Wilson et al., 2015.

claim: 200 µM isopentenyl pyrophosphate (IPP) rescues parasites from the delayed-death activity of 1–3 µM DOX.
source: Prior studies have shown that 200 µM isopentenyl pyrophosphate (IPP), an essential apicoplast product, rescues parasites from the delayed-death activity of 1–3 µM DOX, confirming an apicoplast-specific target (Yeh and DeRisi, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yeh and DeRisi, 2011.

claim: IPP is an essential apicoplast product.
source: Prior studies have shown that 200 µM isopentenyl pyrophosphate (IPP), an essential apicoplast product, rescues parasites from the delayed-death activity of 1–3 µM DOX, confirming an apicoplast-specific target (Yeh and DeRisi, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citation to Yeh and DeRisi, 2011.

claim: IPP rescue of parasites from 1 µM DOX was confirmed in this study.
source: To provide a baseline for comparison, we first used continuous-growth and 48 hr growth-inhibition assays to confirm that IPP rescued parasites from 1 µM DOX (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: DOX concentrations > 5 µM kill parasites with first-cycle activity.
source: we first used continuous-growth and 48 hr growth-inhibition assays to confirm that IPP rescued parasites from 1 µM DOX (Figure 2A) and that DOX concentrations > 5 µM killed parasites with first-cycle activity (Figure 2A-C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1) as previously reported (Dahl et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2A-C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and by citation to Dahl et al., 2006.

claim: IPP shifted the 48 hr EC50 value of DOX from 5 ± 1 to 12 ± 2 µM.
source: We observed that IPP shifted the 48 hr EC50 value of DOX from 5 ± 1 to 12 ± 2 µM (average ± SD of five independent assays, p=0.001 by two-tailed unpaired t-test) (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from five independent assays shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, with statistical analysis.

claim: First-cycle growth defects from 5 to 10 µM DOX reflect an apicoplast-specific mechanism.
source: We observed that IPP shifted the 48 hr EC50 value of DOX from 5 ± 1 to 12 ± 2 µM (average ± SD of five independent assays, p=0.001 by two-tailed unpaired t-test) (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that first-cycle growth defects from 5 to 10 µM DOX reflect an apicoplast-specific mechanism but that DOX concentrations > 10 µM cause off-target defects outside this organelle.
evidence: This is inferred from the IPP rescue data showing EC50 shift.

claim: DOX concentrations > 10 µM cause off-target defects outside the apicoplast.
source: We observed that IPP shifted the 48 hr EC50 value of DOX from 5 ± 1 to 12 ± 2 µM (average ± SD of five independent assays, p=0.001 by two-tailed unpaired t-test) (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that first-cycle growth defects from 5 to 10 µM DOX reflect an apicoplast-specific mechanism but that DOX concentrations > 10 µM cause off-target defects outside this organelle.
evidence: This is inferred from the IPP rescue data showing limited rescue at higher DOX concentrations.

claim: IPP fully or nearly fully rescued parasites from first-cycle growth inhibition by 10 µM DOX.
source: We observed that IPP fully or nearly fully rescued parasites from first-cycle growth inhibition by 10 µM but not 20 or 40 µM Dox (Figure 2A and D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: IPP did not rescue parasites from first-cycle growth inhibition by 20 or 40 µM DOX.
source: We observed that IPP fully or nearly fully rescued parasites from first-cycle growth inhibition by 10 µM but not 20 or 40 µM Dox (Figure 2A and D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: 10 µM DOX kills P. falciparum with first-cycle activity by an apicoplast-specific mechanism.
source: On the basis of IPP rescue, we conclude that 10 µM DOX kills P. falciparum with first-cycle activity by an apicoplast-specific mechanism.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the IPP rescue data presented in the study.

claim: Inhibition of apicoplast biogenesis in the second intraerythrocytic cycle is a hallmark of 1–3 µM DOX-treated P. falciparum.
source: Inhibition of apicoplast biogenesis in the second intraerythrocytic cycle is a hallmark of 1–3 µM DOX-treated P. falciparum, resulting in unviable parasite progeny that fail to inherit the organelle (Dahl et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dahl et al., 2006.

claim: 1–3 µM DOX treatment results in unviable parasite progeny that fail to inherit the apicoplast.
source: Inhibition of apicoplast biogenesis in the second intraerythrocytic cycle is a hallmark of 1–3 µM DOX-treated P. falciparum, resulting in unviable parasite progeny that fail to inherit the organelle (Dahl et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dahl et al., 2006.

claim: IPP rescues parasite viability after the second cycle without rescuing apicoplast inheritance.
source: IPP rescues parasite viability after the second cycle without rescuing apicoplast inheritance, such that third-cycle daughter parasites lack the organelle and accumulate apicoplast-targeted proteins in cytoplasmic vesicles (Yeh and DeRisi, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yeh and DeRisi, 2011.

claim: Third-cycle daughter parasites rescued by IPP lack the apicoplast and accumulate apicoplast-targeted proteins in cytoplasmic vesicles.
source: IPP rescues parasite viability after the second cycle without rescuing apicoplast inheritance, such that third-cycle daughter parasites lack the organelle and accumulate apicoplast-targeted proteins in cytoplasmic vesicles (Yeh and DeRisi, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yeh and DeRisi, 2011.

claim: The apicoplast in 10 µM DOX-treated parasites failed to elongate in the first cycle.
source: In contrast to the second-cycle effects of 1–3 µM DOX, the apicoplast in 10 µM DOX-treated parasites failed to elongate in the first cycle.
evidence: This is based on microscopy observations described in the text and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Rescue by 200 µM IPP produced second-cycle parasite progeny with a dispersed GFP signal indicative of apicoplast loss.
source: Rescue by 200 µM IPP produced second-cycle parasite progeny with a dispersed GFP signal indicative of apicoplast loss (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: 10 µM DOX blocks apicoplast biogenesis in the first cycle.
source: We conclude that 10 µM DOX blocks apicoplast biogenesis in the first cycle.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the microscopy data showing failure of apicoplast elongation.

claim: Treatment with 2 µM DOX, 2 µM clindamycin, and 500 nM azithromycin individually produced major growth defects at the end of the second cycle.
source: Treatment with each antibiotic alone produced major growth defects at the end of the second cycle, as expected for delayed-death activity at these concentrations (Dahl and Rosenthal, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to Dahl and Rosenthal, 2007.

claim: Two- and three-way drug combinations of DOX, clindamycin, and azithromycin caused growth defects that were indistinguishable from individual treatments.
source: Two- and three-way drug combinations caused growth defects that were indistinguishable from individual treatments and provided no evidence for additive, first-cycle activity (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Combinatorial treatment with multiple apicoplast-translation inhibitors provided no evidence for additive, first-cycle activity.
source: Two- and three-way drug combinations caused growth defects that were indistinguishable from individual treatments and provided no evidence for additive, first-cycle activity (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The first-cycle activity of 10 µM DOX is due to a distinct mechanism from the delayed-death mechanism of 1 µM DOX.
source: These results contradict a simple model that 1 and 10 µM DOX act via a common translation-blocking mechanism and suggest that the first-cycle activity of 10 µM DOX is due to a distinct mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of additive effects with combinatorial antibiotic treatment.

claim: Tetracycline antibiotics like DOX tightly chelate a wide variety of di- and trivalent metal ions.
source: Tetracycline antibiotics like DOX tightly chelate a wide variety of di- and trivalent metal ions via their siderophore-like arrangement of exocyclic hydroxyl and carbonyl oxygen atoms (Figure 1), with a reported affinity series of Fe3+>Fe2+>Zn2+>Mg2+>Ca2+ (Albert and Rees, 1956; Nelson, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Albert and Rees, 1956 and Nelson, 1998.

claim: The affinity series of tetracycline for metal ions is Fe3+>Fe2+>Zn2+>Mg2+>Ca2+.
source: Tetracycline antibiotics like DOX tightly chelate a wide variety of di- and trivalent metal ions via their siderophore-like arrangement of exocyclic hydroxyl and carbonyl oxygen atoms (Figure 1), with a reported affinity series of Fe3+>Fe2+>Zn2+>Mg2+>Ca2+ (Albert and Rees, 1956; Nelson, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Albert and Rees, 1956 and Nelson, 1998.

claim: Tetracycline interactions with Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions mediate cellular uptake and binding to biomolecular targets.
source: Indeed, tetracycline interactions with Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions mediate cellular uptake and binding to biomolecular targets such as the tetracycline repressor and 16S rRNA (Nelson, 1998; Orth et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nelson, 1998 and Orth et al., 2000.

claim: 10 µM ZnCl2 did not rescue parasite growth from 10 µM DOX.
source: We failed to observe growth rescue by 10 µM ZnCl2 (toxicity limit [Marvin et al., 2012]) or 500 µM CaCl2 in continuous-growth (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1) or 48 hr growth-inhibition assays (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B, Figure 3C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 500 µM CaCl2 did not rescue parasite growth from 10 µM DOX.
source: We failed to observe growth rescue by 10 µM ZnCl2 (toxicity limit [Marvin et al., 2012]) or 500 µM CaCl2 in continuous-growth (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1) or 48 hr growth-inhibition assays (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B, Figure 3C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 500 µM FeCl3 fully or nearly fully rescued parasites from first-cycle growth inhibition by 10 µM DOX.
source: In contrast, 500 µM FeCl3 (and to a lesser extent 500 µM MgCl2) fully or nearly fully rescued parasites from first-cycle growth inhibition by 10 µM DOX (Figure 3C and D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: 500 µM MgCl2 partially rescued parasites from first-cycle growth inhibition by 10 µM DOX.
source: In contrast, 500 µM FeCl3 (and to a lesser extent 500 µM MgCl2) fully or nearly fully rescued parasites from first-cycle growth inhibition by 10 µM DOX (Figure 3C and D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Partial rescue by FeCl3 was observed at concentrations as low as 50 µM.
source: In contrast, 500 µM FeCl3 (and to a lesser extent 500 µM MgCl2) fully or nearly fully rescued parasites from first-cycle growth inhibition by 10 µM DOX (Figure 3C and D), although partial rescue was observed at FeCl3 concentrations as low as 50 µM (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Parasites treated with 10 µM DOX and 500 µM FeCl3 still succumbed to second-cycle, delayed death.
source: However, parasites treated with 10 µM DOX and 500 µM FeCl3 still succumbed to second-cycle, delayed death (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), as expected for distinct mechanisms of first- and second-cycle DOX activity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 500 µM FeCl3 but not CaCl2 rescued first-cycle apicoplast-branching in 10 µM DOX.
source: We also observed that 500 µM FeCl3 but not CaCl2 rescued first-cycle apicoplast-branching in 10 µM DOX (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: IPP rescued parasite viability in 10 µM DOX but did not restore apicoplast branching.
source: These observations contrast with IPP, which rescued parasite viability in 10 µM DOX but did not restore apicoplast branching (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: FeCl3 did not rescue parasites from the second-cycle effects of 1 µM DOX.
source: We further noted that FeCl3 selectively rescued parasites from the apicoplast-specific, first-cycle growth effects of 10 µM DOX but did not rescue parasites from the second-cycle effects of 1 µM DOX (Figure 3F)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: FeCl3 did not rescue parasites from the off-target effects of 20–40 µM DOX.
source: We further noted that FeCl3 selectively rescued parasites from the apicoplast-specific, first-cycle growth effects of 10 µM DOX but did not rescue parasites from the second-cycle effects of 1 µM DOX (Figure 3F) or the off-target effects of 20–40 µM DOX (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 10 µM DOX kills parasites via a metal-dependent, first-cycle mechanism that blocks apicoplast biogenesis and is distinct from the second-cycle, delayed-death mechanism of 1 µM DOX.
source: We conclude that 10 µM DOX kills parasites via a metal-dependent, first-cycle mechanism that blocks apicoplast biogenesis and is distinct from the second-cycle, delayed-death mechanism of 1 µM DOX.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the iron rescue data and comparison with 1 µM DOX effects.

claim: Tetracyclines bind iron more tightly than other metals, with an equilibrium association constant of 10^10 M−1 for 1:1 chelation of Fe3+ versus 10^4 M−1 for Mg2+.
source: Tetracyclines bind iron more tightly than other metals, with an equilibrium association constant of 1010 M−1 for 1:1 chelation of Fe3+ versus 104 M−1 for Mg2+ (Albert and Rees, 1956).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Albert and Rees, 1956.

claim: The labile iron concentration in the parasite cytoplasm is estimated to be ~1 µM.
source: Although the 500 µM concentration of exogenous FeCl3 required for maximal rescue of parasite growth in 10 µM DOX is large relative to the ~1 µM labile iron concentration estimated for the parasite cytoplasm (Scholl et al., 2005), the intracellular iron concentration achieved by exogenous addition of 500 µM FeCl3 remains unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Scholl et al., 2005.

claim: Mechanisms of iron uptake and trafficking by blood-stage P. falciparum remain sparsely understood.
source: Indeed, mechanisms of iron uptake and trafficking by blood-stage P. falciparum remain sparsely understood (Scholl et al., 2005; Mabeza et al., 1999), especially uptake across the four membranes that surround the apicoplast.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Scholl et al., 2005 and Mabeza et al., 1999.

claim: 500 µM FeCl3 or MgCl2 did not rescue second-cycle parasite death in continuous growth assays with 10 µM DOX.
source: However, 500 µM FeCl3 or MgCl2 did not rescue second-cycle parasite death in continuous growth assays with 10 µM (Figure 3D) or 1 µM DOX (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and 3F.

claim: Exogenous iron resulted in only a small, 1.5 µM shift in EC50 value from 0.5 to 2 µM in a 96 hr growth inhibition assay, in contrast to the 10.5 µM shift provided by IPP.
source: Furthermore, exogenous iron resulted in only a small, 1.5 µM shift in EC50 value from 0.5 to 2 µM in a 96 hr growth inhibition assay, in contrast to the 10.5 µM shift provided by IPP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: DOX uptake into the apicoplast is not substantially perturbed by exogenous iron.
source: These results strongly suggest that DOX uptake into the apicoplast is not substantially perturbed by exogenous iron.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that iron does not rescue second-cycle death.

claim: The inability of 500 µM FeCl3 to rescue parasites from first-cycle activity by ≥20 µM DOX suggests that general uptake of DOX into parasites is not substantially affected by exogenous iron.
source: The inability of 500 µM FeCl3 to rescue parasites from first-cycle activity by ≥20 µM DOX (Figure 3G) further suggests that general uptake of DOX into parasites is not substantially affected by exogenous iron.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Apicoplast biogenesis requires Fe-S cluster synthesis apart from known essential roles in isoprenoid biosynthesis.
source: Indeed, prior work has shown that apicoplast biogenesis requires Fe-S cluster synthesis apart from known essential roles in isoprenoid biosynthesis (Gisselberg et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gisselberg et al., 2013.

claim: Plasmodium growth inhibited by deferoxamine (DFO) could be partially rescued by IPP.
source: Consistent with a general mechanism that labile-iron chelation can block apicoplast biogenesis, we observed in preliminary studies that Plasmodium growth inhibited by the highly specific iron chelator, deferoxamine (DFO) (Mabeza et al., 1999), could be partially rescued by IPP, fully rescued by exogenous FeCl3, and involved a first-cycle defect in apicoplast elongation (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by preliminary experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Plasmodium growth inhibited by deferoxamine (DFO) could be fully rescued by exogenous FeCl3.
source: Consistent with a general mechanism that labile-iron chelation can block apicoplast biogenesis, we observed in preliminary studies that Plasmodium growth inhibited by the highly specific iron chelator, deferoxamine (DFO) (Mabeza et al., 1999), could be partially rescued by IPP, fully rescued by exogenous FeCl3, and involved a first-cycle defect in apicoplast elongation (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by preliminary experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Plasmodium growth inhibited by deferoxamine (DFO) involved a first-cycle defect in apicoplast elongation.
source: Consistent with a general mechanism that labile-iron chelation can block apicoplast biogenesis, we observed in preliminary studies that Plasmodium growth inhibited by the highly specific iron chelator, deferoxamine (DFO) (Mabeza et al., 1999), could be partially rescued by IPP, fully rescued by exogenous FeCl3, and involved a first-cycle defect in apicoplast elongation (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by preliminary experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Lipoic acid and isoprenoid biosynthesis in the apicoplast require Fe/S-cluster biosynthesis for activity.
source: To more broadly evaluate the impact of DOX on iron availability in the apicoplast, we are developing protein-based probes of lipoic acid and isoprenoid biosynthesis, as these two apicoplast-dependent processes require Fe/S-cluster biosynthesis for activity (Gisselberg et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gisselberg et al., 2013.

claim: DOX mechanisms include a delayed, second-cycle defect at 1–3 µM that likely reflects inhibition of 70S apicoplast ribosomes.
source: These mechanisms include a delayed, second-cycle defect at 1–3 µM DOX that likely reflects inhibition of 70S apicoplast ribosomes, a first-cycle iron-dependent defect within the apicoplast that uniquely operates at 8–10 µM DOX, and a first-cycle iron-independent mechanism outside the apicoplast at ≥20 µM DOX (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: DOX mechanisms include a first-cycle iron-dependent defect within the apicoplast that uniquely operates at 8–10 µM DOX.
source: These mechanisms include a delayed, second-cycle defect at 1–3 µM DOX that likely reflects inhibition of 70S apicoplast ribosomes, a first-cycle iron-dependent defect within the apicoplast that uniquely operates at 8–10 µM DOX, and a first-cycle iron-independent mechanism outside the apicoplast at ≥20 µM DOX (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: DOX mechanisms include a first-cycle iron-independent mechanism outside the apicoplast at ≥20 µM DOX.
source: These mechanisms include a delayed, second-cycle defect at 1–3 µM DOX that likely reflects inhibition of 70S apicoplast ribosomes, a first-cycle iron-dependent defect within the apicoplast that uniquely operates at 8–10 µM DOX, and a first-cycle iron-independent mechanism outside the apicoplast at ≥20 µM DOX (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Current 100–200 mg doses of DOX achieve peak human serum concentrations of 6–8 µM over the first six hours which then decrease to 1–2 µM over 24 hr.
source: Pharmacokinetic studies indicate that current 100–200 mg doses of DOX achieve peak human serum concentrations of 6–8 µM over the first six hours which then decrease to 1–2 µM over 24 hr (Newton et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Newton et al., 2005.

claim: Both apicoplast-specific mechanisms of DOX likely operate over the 1-8 µM concentration range and contribute to parasite death.
source: Although current DOX treatment regimens result in delayed parasite clearance in vivo, both apicoplast-specific mechanisms of DOX likely operate over this concentration range and contribute to parasite death (Dahl et al., 2006).
evidence: This is inferred from the pharmacokinetic data and the experimental findings, with citation to Dahl et al., 2006.

claim: Multiple mechanisms of DOX, together with limited antimalarial use in the field, may explain why parasites with stable DOX resistance have not emerged.
source: These multiple mechanisms of DOX, together with limited antimalarial use of DOX in the field, may explain why parasites with stable DOX resistance have not emerged (Conrad and Rosenthal, 2019; Gaillard et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the findings, with citations to Conrad and Rosenthal, 2019 and Gaillard et al., 2015.

claim: There has been a prevailing view that delayed-death activity is a fundamental limitation of antibiotics like DOX that block apicoplast maintenance.
source: There has been a prevailing view in the literature that delayed-death activity is a fundamental limitation of antibiotics like DOX that block apicoplast maintenance (Ramya et al., 2007; Kennedy et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ramya et al., 2007 and Kennedy et al., 2019.

claim: DOX is not an intrinsically slow-acting antimalarial drug.
source: Our results emphasize that DOX is not an intrinsically slow-acting antimalarial drug and support the emerging paradigm (Boucher and Yeh, 2019; Amberg-Johnson et al., 2017; Uddin et al., 2018) that inhibition of apicoplast biogenesis can defy the delayed-death phenotype to kill parasites on a faster time-scale.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental findings showing first-cycle activity at 10 µM DOX.

claim: Inhibition of apicoplast biogenesis can defy the delayed-death phenotype to kill parasites on a faster time-scale.
source: Our results emphasize that DOX is not an intrinsically slow-acting antimalarial drug and support the emerging paradigm (Boucher and Yeh, 2019; Amberg-Johnson et al., 2017; Uddin et al., 2018) that inhibition of apicoplast biogenesis can defy the delayed-death phenotype to kill parasites on a faster time-scale.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boucher and Yeh, 2019; Amberg-Johnson et al., 2017; Uddin et al., 2018.

claim: The apicoplast may be especially susceptible to therapeutic strategies that interfere with acquisition and utilization of iron.
source: The first-cycle, iron-dependent impacts of 10 µM DOX or 15 µM DFO on apicoplast biogenesis also suggest that this organelle may be especially susceptible to therapeutic strategies that interfere with acquisition and utilization of iron, perhaps due to limited uptake of exogenous iron and/or limited iron storage mechanisms in the apicoplast.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the experimental findings.

claim: 500–600 mg doses of DOX in humans achieve sustained serum DOX concentrations ≥ 5 µM for 24–48 hr with little or no increase in adverse effects.
source: Prior studies indicate that 500–600 mg doses in humans achieve sustained serum DOX concentrations ≥ 5 µM for 24–48 hr with little or no increase in adverse effects (Marlin and Cheng, 1979; Adadevoh et al., 1976).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Marlin and Cheng, 1979 and Adadevoh et al., 1976.

claim: DOX is currently contraindicated for long-term prophylaxis in pregnant women and young children due to concerns about impacts on fetal development and infant tooth discoloration.
source: DOX is currently contraindicated for long-term prophylaxis in pregnant women and young children, two of the major at-risk populations for malaria, due to concerns about impacts on fetal development and infant tooth discoloration, respectively, based on observed toxicities for other tetracyclines (Gaillard et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gaillard et al., 2018.

claim: Recent studies suggest that fetal development and tooth discoloration effects are not associated with short-term DOX use.
source: Recent studies suggest that these effects are not associated with short-term DOX use (Gaillard et al., 2018; Todd et al., 2015; Cross et al., 2016), and additional tests can define the safety parameters that would govern short-term use of DOX for treatment in these populations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gaillard et al., 2018; Todd et al., 2015; Cross et al., 2016.

claim: Recent development of tetracycline derivatives with improved activities may provide another option to deploy this class of antibiotics for antimalarial treatment.
source: Recent development of tetracycline derivatives with improved activities may provide another option to deploy this important class of antibiotics for antimalarial treatment (Draper et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Draper et al., 2013.

claim: 10 µM DOX blocks apicoplast biogenesis in the first cycle and is rescued by isopentenyl pyrophosphate, confirming an apicoplast-specific mechanism.
source: We report that 10 µM DOX blocks apicoplast biogenesis in the first cycle and is rescued by isopentenyl pyrophosphate, an essential apicoplast product, confirming an apicoplast-specific mechanism.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental finding from the abstract.

claim: Exogenous iron rescues parasites and apicoplast biogenesis from first- but not second-cycle effects of 10 µM DOX.
source: Exogenous iron rescues parasites and apicoplast biogenesis from first- but not second-cycle effects of 10 µM DOX, revealing that first-cycle activity involves a metal-dependent mechanism distinct from the delayed-death mechanism.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental finding from the abstract.

claim: First-cycle activity of 10 µM DOX involves a metal-dependent mechanism distinct from the delayed-death mechanism.
source: Exogenous iron rescues parasites and apicoplast biogenesis from first- but not second-cycle effects of 10 µM DOX, revealing that first-cycle activity involves a metal-dependent mechanism distinct from the delayed-death mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the iron rescue data.
